newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW - Philippine bond issue seen early 97.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Philippine bond issue seen early 97.

text.p: The Philippines' Secretary of Finance Roberto de Ocampo said on Tuesday he expected the Philippines to make a Europeso or Yankee Bond issue in the first half of 1997.

"I think it is likely to take place in the first half of next year, perhaps the Euro-peso before the Yankee bond or perhaps the Euro-peso and a Yankee bond being floated instead by either the private sector or by government corporations who are going to be taking advantage of the benchmarks we have set this year by going into the Samurai (markets) and Brady (bond) exchanges successfully," De Ocampo told Reuters in an interview.
De Ocampo is in Australia for the National Trade and Investment Outlook Conference.

De Ocampo said any issues would not be carried out in 1996 because the Philippines had already made two issues this year -- a US$1.9 billion swap of Brady bonds into uncollateralised Eurobonds in September and a US$450 million Samurai issue in July.
The Philippines' budget situation was also not in urgent need of funding and there would not be enough time to do the usual roadshows to promote such issues, he said.
De Ocampo also said he expected the ratings agencies to look at upgrading the Philippines sovereign debt ratings again in the next year.
He referred to a recent Merrill Lynch report which said the Philippines could expect a credit rating upgrade very soon if it passed controversial tax reforms.
New taxes on beer and cigarettes were signed into law late last month and are expected to raise six billion to 6.5 billion pesos extra every year.

"Now it's passed, I wouldn't be surprised if the credit rating agencies come trooping back to Manila this coming year, because the country would have at the end of the year shown it's on a sustained growth path and by this time next year we would have exited the IMF for the first time in 30 years," he said.

A three-year International Monetary Fund (IMF) supervisory programme which set the Philippines a range of economic goals is due to end in June 1997 and the Philippines has already met most of these goals.

"All of this points very forcefully to a credit upgrade," he said, adding that international investors had already made their judgments by pricing Philippine debt instruments at investment grade levels.
In February, Moody's Investors Service upgraded the Philippines' long term foreign currency loan rating to Ba2 from Ba3, while Standard & Poors Corp raised its rating to BB from BB-minus.
